title: French experts urge safety checks before consumer AI chatbots reach the market
excerpt: A commission reporting to France's president makes 18 recommendations, including checks before launch, limits on manipulative design and prior approval for AI toys.

sources.title: Élysée: Remise du rapport de la Commission d'experts « IA générative et vulnérabilités »
Élysée: Rapport « Protéger sans empêcher : nos vulnérabilités à l'ère de l'IA générative » (PDF)
France-Soir: Macron considère l'interdiction des IA dangereuses pour les enfants
Le Filia: Emmanuel Macron veut interdire l'IA lorsqu'elle présente un risque pour les enfants

body_html:
An expert commission in France has recommended that AI chatbots sold to the general public should be assessed before they reach the market, to show that they do not exploit or worsen the vulnerabilities of the people who use them. The report was handed to President Emmanuel Macron on 10 November 2026 and published by the Élysée, the French presidency.

Who wrote it

The commission, called "Generative AI and vulnerabilities", was set up by France's Council for AI and Digital Affairs (Conseil de l'IA et du numérique), an advisory body. It has nine independent experts and is led by AI researcher Serena Villata and psychiatrists Raphaël Gaillard and Amine Benyamina. According to the Élysée, it held 55 hearings with health professionals, researchers, companies and child protection groups. Its report is titled Protéger sans empêcher, which translates as "Protect without preventing".

The main recommendations

The report makes 18 recommendations, nine of them marked as priorities. Among them:

  • No manipulative design: ban design techniques in conversational AI that exploit users' vulnerabilities to create dependence or keep them engaged, and limit excessive flattery and human-like behaviour that can blur the line between person and machine.
  • Checks before launch: consumer generative AI systems, including chatbots built into social networks, would need an assessment before they can be sold in the EU. Professional-only systems are not covered by this proposal.
  • Checks after launch: continuous monitoring, periodic re-evaluation, a fresh assessment after each major model change, and a way to raise alerts.
  • Independent evaluation: an interdisciplinary testing and audit system, with France's national AI evaluation institute (INESIA) and the EU AI Office strengthened, and authorised researchers given access to relevant data.
  • Minors: a high level of safety by default for any system that children can use.
  • AI toys: prior authorisation before toys with generative AI can be sold, based on testing designed around risks to children, with age limits set through a consensus conference.
  • Advertising and inferences: a ban on hidden advertising and covert commercial influence, and a duty to tell users which personal characteristics a service may infer about them.
  • Liability: clear provider responsibility, without a broad defence that a risk could not have been foreseen.

What happens next

The report is advice, not law. The Élysée page does not set out a timetable or say which recommendations the government will adopt. Several proposals, such as checks before sale across the EU, would need action at European level. France-Soir reports that Mr Macron has said he favours banning certain AI uses that could harm children, especially chatbots and connected toys, and wants rules agreed at EU level rather than country by country. Le Filia reports that the government has not yet said which measures will follow.

Some of the ground is already covered by EU law. The EU AI Act already bans AI that exploits vulnerabilities linked to age, under specific conditions, and requires chatbots to make clear that people are talking to a machine. The commission's proposals would go further by asking providers to show safety before launch rather than after problems appear.

Why it matters for staying in charge

The report touches several of the 10 Humasure Directives. Limits on dependence-building design match D7 No manipulation. Clear signals that a chatbot is not a person relate to D4 Honest identity. Rules on inferred personal data match D5 Private by default, and clear provider liability matches D9 Accountable.

The central idea, testing before a product reaches people and checking it again as it changes, is the same idea behind independent safety certification. Whatever France decides, anyone choosing a chatbot or AI toy for a family can already ask the maker how it was tested; our questions to ask page lists some starting points.
